title: Creatives and the sports calendar
summary: How to plan spend around fixtures and build sportsbook and casino creatives that convert without misleading anyone. You will localise for each geo, run a creative pipeline with fatigue rules, and review every ad before it goes live.

lessons.title: The sports calendar is your media plan
objectives: By the end you can build a fixture calendar for your geos and weight budgets by event.
By the end you can convert kickoff times into local time for each African geo.
By the end you can apply starting rules for event-day budget boosts and pull-backs.

steps.p: In sports betting, demand is not flat. It rises before big fixtures and falls in quiet weeks. Ad costs, click-through rates and deposit intent all move with the schedule. A buyer who plans around fixtures spends more on days that convert and less on days that do not. A buyer who ignores them pays the same money for weaker days.

d.s: Plan spend around the schedule, not around your mood.

steps.h: The layers of a sports calendar
steps.p: Think of the calendar in layers. A weekly league rhythm sits underneath everything. Tournaments sit on top for a few weeks at a time. Local leagues and other sports fill gaps. Off-season weeks need a different plan, often more casino or a pause.
steps.more: Which events matter depends on the geo. In Nigeria, Ghana and Kenya, the big European football leagues usually lead. In South Africa, rugby and cricket also matter alongside football. In Cameroon, French-language coverage and French football carry weight. Always confirm fixture dates from the official league or federation site, because schedules move for television, weather and security reasons.

steps.h: Worked example: dearer CPM, cheaper FTD
steps.p: Example: a quiet Tuesday against a derby Saturday in the same geo. CPM is 30% higher on Saturday, but more people click, so each click costs less. With the same click-to-FTD rate, the cost per FTD is lower on the expensive day.
steps.more: Check the maths. Tuesday: $2.00 ÷ (1000 × 0.015) = $2.00 ÷ 15 = $0.133 per click. $0.133 ÷ 0.008 = $16.67 per FTD. Saturday: $2.60 ÷ 24 = $0.108 per click. $0.108 ÷ 0.008 = $13.54 per FTD. The lesson: never judge a day on CPM alone. The number that pays you is cost per qualified FTD, which Module 5 covers.
steps.say: Here's a worked example: a quiet Tuesday against a derby Saturday in the same geo. Read the table. Saturday's C P M is thirty percent higher, but C T R, click-through rate, rises from one point five to two point four percent, so each click costs less. With the same click to F T D rate of zero point eight percent, the cost per F T D is sixteen sixty seven on Tuesday, but only thirteen fifty four on Saturday. So never judge a day on C P M alone.

steps.p: Here is how to build a simple fixture sheet in any spreadsheet. One row per event, one column per geo. Tag priority so the budget rule can read it.

steps.title: Open the official sources
steps.text: Use the official league, federation or tournament site for dates. Do not rely on a fan page or memory.

steps.title: Add one row per event
steps.text: Date, kickoff in UK or venue time, competition, teams, and which geos care.

steps.title: Convert to local time
steps.text: Add a column per geo with the local kickoff time. This is when your ads should already be live.

steps.title: Tag priority and weight
steps.text: Priority A gets weight 1.5, B gets 1.2, normal days 1.0. The weight multiplies your base daily budget.

steps.say: Let's build a simple fixture sheet, step by step. Step one: open the official sources, the league, federation or tournament site, never a fan page or memory, and re-check dates weekly. Step two: add one row per event, with the date, kickoff time, competition, teams, and which geos care. Step three: convert to local time, with a column per geo, because that's when your ads should already be live. Step four: tag priority and weight. Priority A gets one point five, B gets one point two, normal days one point oh.

steps.p: UK clocks change in late March and late October. Most African geos do not change clocks. So the same UK kickoff lands at a different local hour in summer and winter. Check your sheet when the UK clocks change.
steps.more: Ghana is on UTC+0, Nigeria and Cameroon on UTC+1, South Africa on UTC+2, Kenya on UTC+3. UK winter time is UTC+0 and summer time is UTC+1. Example: a 20:00 UK winter kickoff is 23:00 in Nairobi. A late kickoff in Kenya means fewer people awake for in-play, so your Kenyan budget may peak earlier in the evening than your Ghanaian budget.
steps.say: Here's a detail that trips people up. U K clocks change in late March and late October, but most African geos don't change their clocks. So the same U K kickoff lands at a different local hour in summer and winter. Read the table. A twenty hundred U K kickoff in winter is twenty one hundred in Nigeria and twenty three hundred in Kenya. In summer, it's an hour earlier. Check your sheet whenever U K clocks change.

steps.p: Your base daily budget is what you spend on a normal day when results are on target. The event weight lifts it for priority fixtures. Keep weights modest; a big jump can unsettle delivery.
steps.more: Example: base $50 a day. A priority A derby has weight 1.5, so the event-day budget is $50 × 1.5 = $75. A priority B cup night has weight 1.2, so $60. Many buyers run a separate event campaign for the extra spend instead of editing the evergreen campaign, because large or frequent budget edits can push an ad set back into learning on Meta. We are not certain how the current learning-phase rules treat each edit; check Meta's Help Center before relying on it.

For example, with a fifty dollar base, a priority A derby at one point five gives seventy five dollars. Keep weights modest, because a big jump can unsettle delivery. Many buyers run a separate event campaign for the extra spend, but we're not certain how current learning-phase rules treat each edit, so check Meta's help centre.

steps.p: Starting rules to adapt with your own data. They stop a matchday from turning into an expensive guess. Write them on your fixture sheet so the decision is made before the match starts, not during it.
steps.more: Why a 3-day window? Many bettors register on matchday and deposit a day or two later, and network postbacks can lag. Example: target CPA $20. The event campaign spends $40 before kickoff with 0 FTDs. That is 2 × target, so you return to base. If instead it has 2 FTDs, you hold and read it again after 3 days.

Cap the boost at +50% of base for the day
Start the boost 4 to 6 hours before local kickoff
If event spend hits 2 × target CPA with 0 FTDs, return to base
Back to base budget the next morning
Judge event ad sets on a 3-day window, not matchday alone
steps.say: Here are starting rules for event days, to adapt with your own data. Boost only if the last seven days are at or under target C P A, cost per acquisition. Cap the boost at fifty percent above base. Start it four to six hours before local kickoff. If event spend hits two times target C P A with zero F T Ds, return to base. Go back to base the next morning. And judge event ad sets on a three day window, because many bettors deposit a day or two after registering.

steps.h: Why creative is the lever and the risk
steps.p: On paid social, the creative decides most of your cost per FTD. In gambling it also decides whether the ad is approved, whether the operator keeps you, and whether a regulator ever writes to you. One misleading line can cost more than a month of profit.

d.b: Your best lever is also your biggest risk
d.s: Write ads you could defend to a regulator.

steps.say: On paid social, the creative decides most of your cost per F T D, first-time deposit. In gambling, it also decides whether the ad is approved, whether the operator keeps you, and whether a regulator ever writes to you. One misleading line can cost more than a month of profit. So your best lever is also your biggest risk. Write ads you could defend to a regulator.

steps.p: These angles work without stretching the truth. Each one gives a real reason to act today. Pick one angle per creative so you can tell which one works.

Local payment: deposit and withdraw with local methods. Welcome offer: the offer plus its key terms on screen. And content: a short preview, form guide or stat. Pick one angle per creative so you can tell which works. Feature and payment angles only work if they're true for that operator in that geo.

steps.h: Why you can never claim betting earns money
steps.p: Odds include the bookmaker's margin. Implied probability is 1 divided by decimal odds. Add both sides of a market and the total is over 100%. That extra is the operator's edge, so bettors as a group lose over time.
steps.more: Example: a two-way market priced 1.90 and 1.90. 1 ÷ 1.90 = 52.6% for each side. Together that is 105.3%. The 5.3% above 100% is the bookmaker's margin. A bettor who stakes $10 on both sides gets back $19 whichever side wins, a $1 loss on $20 staked. This is why 'make money betting' claims are false for the average player and banned by most codes.
d: 1 ÷ decimal odds
Implied probability
steps.say: Here's why you can never claim betting earns money. Odds include the bookmaker's margin. Look at the equation: one divided by decimal odds gives implied probability. Example: a two-way market priced at one point nine on both sides. Each side is fifty two point six percent, and together that's one hundred and five point three percent. That extra five point three percent is the operator's edge. Stake ten dollars on both sides and you get back nineteen, whichever wins. So bettors as a group lose over time.

steps.p: Most rejected gambling ads fail on the same few claims. Learn the replacements by heart. If a line on the left appears anywhere in your ad, on screen, in the voiceover or in the caption, the ad is not ready.
steps.more: Some codes set the actor age above 18. In the UK, for example, people in gambling ads must not be, or seem to be, under 25. African codes differ by country. Using clearly adult people everywhere is a simple way to stay inside the strictest rule.

Never make money daily or quit your job; say bet for fun, set a limit. Never free money, no risk; say welcome offer, wagering applies, T and Cs. Never young-looking actors; use clearly adult actors, twenty five plus is safer. Never famous players without rights; use generic fans or approved assets. If a left-column line appears anywhere, the ad isn't ready.

steps.h: Worked example: cost per qualified FTD
steps.p: Example: the offer angle brings cheap FTDs but many are bonus chasers who never qualify. The fixture angle costs more per FTD but more of them qualify. You are paid on qualified FTDs, so the fixture angle wins.
steps.more: Cost per qualified FTD = cost per FTD ÷ qualified share. Fixture: $16 ÷ 0.80 = $20.00. Offer: $12 ÷ 0.50 = $24.00. Feature: $18 ÷ 0.85 = $21.18. Example payout $30 per qualified FTD: the fixture angle leaves $10 per qualified FTD, the offer angle $6. Module 5 shows how to get the qualified share from your operator reports.

steps.h: The casino products you will promote
steps.p: Know what each product is before you write about it. The honest description is also the compliant one. If you cannot explain in one sentence how a game decides the outcome, do not advertise it yet.
d: Slots|random number generator decides each spin
Live casino|real dealers streamed, house edge applies
Crash and instant games|multiplier rises then stops at random
Table games|roulette, blackjack, baccarat with fixed edges
Jackpots|rare large prizes funded by many players
steps.say: Know what each product is before you write about it. Look at the cards. Slots: a random number generator decides each spin. Live casino: real dealers streamed, and the house edge still applies. Crash and instant games: a multiplier rises, then stops at random. Table games: roulette, blackjack and baccarat, with fixed edges. And jackpots: rare large prizes funded by many players. If you can't explain in one sentence how a game decides the outcome, don't advertise it yet.

steps.p: RTP (return to player) is the share of money staked that a game pays back over a very long run. The rest is the house edge. Over a short session, results swing widely, but the average always leans to the house.
steps.more: Example: a slot with 96% RTP. A player wagers $100 in total across many spins. Expected loss is $100 × (1 − 0.96) = $4. Some sessions end up, many end down, the long-run average is a $4 loss per $100 wagered. European roulette has 37 pockets and pays as if there were 36, so the house edge is 1 ÷ 37 = 2.7%. RTP figures are set by the game provider and published by the operator; quote them only from the operator's own game page.
d: Amount wagered
(1 − RTP)
Expected loss
steps.say: R T P, return to player, is the share of money staked that a game pays back over a very long run. The rest is the house edge. Look at the equation: amount wagered times one minus R T P equals expected loss. Example: a slot with ninety six percent R T P. Wager one hundred dollars in total, and the expected loss is four dollars. Short sessions swing widely, but the average always leans to the house. Quote R T P figures only from the operator's own game page.

steps.h: Worked example: what a bonus really costs
steps.p: Example: a 100% deposit match with a wagering requirement. The headline sounds like free money. The maths shows why ads must state the key terms next to the offer.
steps.more: To release the $20 bonus the player must stake $600 in total. At 96% RTP the expected loss on $600 of wagering is $24, which is more than the bonus itself. On average the player ends $4 worse off than if there were no bonus, before counting time and any game restrictions. That is why 'free $20' is misleading. Write 'Welcome bonus up to $20. 30× wagering. T&Cs apply.' Terms vary by operator; copy them exactly from the operator.
steps.say: Here's what a bonus really costs, as an example. Read the table. The player deposits twenty dollars and gets a one hundred percent match, another twenty. But the wagering is thirty times the bonus, so six hundred dollars to wager. At ninety six percent R T P, the expected loss on six hundred is twenty four dollars, more than the bonus itself. Net expectation: minus four dollars. That's why free twenty dollars is misleading, and ads must state the key terms next to the offer.

steps.more: Crash-game 'predictors' and signal groups are a common scam in African markets. Outcomes are random and cannot be predicted from previous rounds. Promoting them misleads players, breaks platform policy and will get you removed by any licensed operator.

steps.p: Sportsbook creatives age fast. A fixture creative is useless after the final whistle, and even evergreen ads tire as the same people see them again and again. Without a steady pipeline you end up with nothing fresh on the biggest days and pay more for every FTD.

steps.say: Sportsbook creatives age fast. A fixture creative is useless after the final whistle, and even evergreen ads tire as the same people see them again and again. Without a steady pipeline, you end up with nothing fresh on the biggest days, and you pay more for every F T D, first-time deposit. So plan production like the fixture list.

steps.p: A simple weekly loop. Briefs come from last week's data and next week's fixtures. Everything passes review before it is uploaded. Fixture creatives for a weekend must be uploaded and approved by Friday, because reviews can take hours or longer.

steps.say: Here's a simple weekly loop. Monday, review last week's data. Tuesday, brief the batch, using that data and next week's fixtures. Wednesday to Thursday, produce. Friday, compliance review. Before kickoff, upload. And afterwards, log the results. Fixture creatives for a weekend must be uploaded and approved by Friday, because reviews can take hours or longer.

steps.p: Rotate formats as well as hooks. The same angle in a new format often beats a brand new angle, because you keep what already works and only change how it looks. Test each format with the same fixture first.

10-second fixture clip|kickoff countdown, no outcome claims
Talking-head preview|clearly adult presenter, form guide

steps.say: Rotate formats as well as hooks. Look at the cards. An odds card, a static with the fixture, time and eighteen plus line. A ten second fixture clip with a kickoff countdown and no outcome claims. A talking-head preview with a clearly adult presenter. A feature demo, a screen recording of live betting or cash out. And a carousel of this weekend's fixtures. The same angle in a new format often beats a brand new angle, because you keep what already works.

steps.h: Worked example: a batch and its budget
steps.p: Example: a batch of six creatives for one geo, three angles in two formats. The test budget comes straight from the kill rule. Work out the budget before anyone starts producing, so the batch size matches what you can afford to test.
steps.more: If $360 is more than you can lose this week, test four creatives instead of six, not six creatives with less spend each. A creative judged on half the needed spend tells you almost nothing. Testing fewer ideas properly beats testing many ideas badly.

The judge line is three times target, sixty. Three angles in two formats gives six creatives. So the full test budget is three hundred and sixty dollars, or at least two hundred and forty if most die early. steps.h: Worked example: the cost of one bad ad
